title: Multi-Region Architecture
description: Design global architectures using Route 53, CloudFront, and multi-region database replication for active-active patterns.

data.text: A **multi-region architecture** distributes your application across two or more AWS regions. If one region fails, users can be routed to another region automatically.
Route 53 is AWS's DNS service. It can route users to the nearest or healthiest region. CloudFront caches content at edge locations around the world, reducing latency for static assets and APIs.

data.caption: Multi-region setup with Route 53 and CloudFront
data.definition:
flowchart TD
    A[Users Worldwide] --> B[CloudFront CDN]
    A --> C[Route 53 DNS]
    C -->|Health Check| C
    C -->|Primary: Region A| D[Region A: ALB + EC2 + RDS]
    C -->|Failover: Region B| E[Region B: ALB + EC2 + RDS]
    D --> F[DynamoDB Global Table]
    E --> F
    B -->|Cache Hit| G[Edge Locations]
    G --> A
    B -->|Cache Miss| D

data.title: Replication Strategies
items: **DynamoDB Global Tables** — multi-master, multi-region NoSQL tables
**S3 Cross-Region Replication** — copies objects between buckets in different regions
**RDS Cross-Region Read Replicas** — read-only copies for disaster recovery
**Aurora Global Database** — cross-region replication for Aurora with < 1-second lag

data.title: Architecture Tip
data.text: Use Route 53 latency-based routing for active-active setups and health-check-based routing for active-passive failover.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Multi-region architectures protect against region-wide outages
Route 53 routes users based on health and latency
CloudFront reduces latency with edge caching
Global tables and cross-region replication keep data synchronized
